summary: Carrie Andrews, an American co-founder of a UK biocatalyst engineering company, argues that Rishi Sunak's September 2023 decision to delay the UK's net-zero timeline by at least five years undermines climate tech startups. She says innovation depends on early government support and consistent policy. She calls for consistency in macroeconomic, tax (notably R&D tax credits) and climate policy.
one_line: A climate tech founder argues the UK's delay of its net-zero timeline under Sunak creates uncertainty and calls for consistent macroeconomic, tax and climate policy.
key_facts: Rishi Sunak spoke to the press on September 20, 2023, under the lectern slogan "Long-term decisions for a brighter future."
Sunak pushed back the British net-zero transition timeline by at least five years.
The author and her colleagues are Americans who chose to build a biocatalyst engineering company in the U.K.
Her company is trying to move industry away from reliance on fossil fuels to make chemicals.
Chancellor Jeremy Hunt said in January 2023 that he wanted the world's tech entrepreneurs, life science innovators and clean energy companies to come to the U.K.
The author argues that solar panels, microchips, mobile phones and the internet all depended on early government funding, subsidies, encouragement and infrastructure.
An EV battery business has seen market demand for its output slide back by five years because of the policy reversal; the author notes that even giants like Ford are frustrated.
The author's first demand is a consistent macroeconomic policy, since the global economic contraction has made it hard for startups to raise money.
The author's second demand is a consistent tax policy, centered on R&D tax credits that effectively returned about a third of R&D spending to small research-intensive companies.
The government announced last year it would scrap the R&D tax credit, but lobbying led by the Startup Coalition preserved a portion at the last minute.
The third and most important demand is a consistent climate policy, since climate tech launch plans are aligned around decarbonization timelines.
The author's conclusion is that "Inconsistency breeds uncertainty," which will damage economic confidence, cost jobs and delay action.
